one_liner: C++20 shared-memory pub/sub framework passing slab handles over SPSC rings; beat Protobuf+ZeroMQ in author's six-process pipeline benchmark.
what_it_does: Mino is a Linux messaging framework for one host and across hosts. A publisher builds the message directly in a POSIX shared-memory slab and sends only a 128-byte index slot holding a relative handle. Local subscribers read the payload in place, and a TCP bridge re-encodes it into a compact canonical wire format for remote nodes. It is not a ZeroMQ drop-in because it has no sockets or socket patterns. You use either SimpleNode (create or open a named shm segment, advertise or subscribe to topics in SPSC, MPSC or broadcast mode, publish bytes or POD types, poll for borrowed views) or the typed Publisher<T>/Subscriber<T> API over types that the minoc compiler generates from a .mino IDL. Calls are noexcept and return errors as Status/Result.
how_it_is_fast: The control path and the data path are separate. A cache-line-aligned SPSC index ring keeps the producer and consumer cursors on separate cache lines and needs no CAS. It carries ShmHandle offsets into a central slab allocator that uses fixed-size classes and a sharded atomic bitmap, so allocate and free are O(1). Frames are generated with a fixed layout, so a same-host hop needs no Protobuf-style encode/parse and no socket syscall, and subscribers spin on the ring with yield instead of blocking in the kernel. In the benchmarked commit (c977bd1), each forwarding stage still copied the payload out and into a new slab, so the measured win comes from skipping serialization and socket I/O. True zero-copy forwarding (the 'exclusive hop', TakeExclusive -> PublishLocal) landed later in a1b76c3, and docs/benchmarks has no end-to-end numbers for it.
when_to_use: Linux x86-64, several processes on one host in a fixed pipeline (robotics or autonomous-driving stages, sensor fusion) where Protobuf+ZeroMQ encode/parse per hop dominates latency.

Small, frequent messages (about 256 B): 5.8x lower saturated p50 than Protobuf+ZeroMQ on the KVM run. The author's earlier paced 100 Hz run on an i9-9900KS gave 19 us vs 586 us p50 end to end over five hops.

Typed fixed-layout messages up to about 1 MiB where you want deterministic O(1) slab allocation and explicit crash recovery of leases, pins and allocation journals (SimpleNode::Recover(), a journal-backed Subscriber).
Systems that need one C++ API and one IDL for same-host SHM and a cross-host TCP bridge, with optional TLS 1.3 mTLS or frame AEAD.
Teams that already build with Bazel/Bzlmod and C++20 and control every process that attaches to the segment.
when_not_to_use: Anything other than Linux x86-64 in production. AArch64 is unqualified (cross-build/QEMU only), and macOS is only for compiling and non-persistent-SHM tests.
When you need ZeroMQ's feature set: REQ/REP, ROUTER/DEALER, bindings for many languages, brokerless TCP across hosts as the primary path. Mino is C++-only pub/sub and work queues.

Cross-host throughput. In the author's one-round two-host run, Mino TCP did 28.2k msg/s at 256 B vs Cyclone DDS's 51.5k. In the one-host six-process smoke, Mino TCP (0.855 ms p50) was only slightly ahead of Cyclone DDS (0.97 ms).
Large payloads. The advantage shrinks to about 2x saturated (1.35x paced) at 1 MiB, and Fast DDS had higher 64 KiB throughput (3571 vs 2925 msg/s).

Production-critical use today. The project is about 2 months old, has one author and no releases, every ADR is ACCEPTED but none VALIDATED or FROZEN, the hardware and clean-ref qualification gates are open, and September commits are still fixing CI race conditions.

integration.form: static lib (Bazel/Bzlmod targets built from source; no CMake, no releases)
integration.dependencies: OpenSSL 3.5.5 (source-built via BCR, production TLS), spdlog 1.15.3, toml++ 3.4.0; minoc codegen for IDL types; ZeroMQ, Protobuf, Fast DDS and Cyclone DDS are benchmark-only
integration.min_toolchain: C++20, Bazel 7.4.1; CI uses GCC 12 and hermetic Clang/LLVM 18.1.8
integration.platforms: Linux x86-64 only for production (ADR-0001); requires lock-free 64-bit atomics; AArch64 and macOS not qualified
integration.thread_safety: SPSC channels require exactly one producer and one consumer (thread or process). MPSC and broadcast (up to 64 subscribers) topic modes exist. Per-object thread safety of Publisher/Subscriber is not documented.

gotchas: Segments are sized as ring capacity x maximum payload. 1 MiB x 64 slots needs about 768 MiB, and the author's smoke run hit SIGBUS on a 64 MiB /dev/shm. Newer code fails closed via posix_fallocate, and the pipeline benchmark falls back to a file-backed mapping.

Waiting burns CPU. Subscriber::Poll loops on std::this_thread::yield() and a kBlock publisher spins with a pause instruction. The design doc lists spin-then-park and futex wait strategies, but code search found no futex use in the source.

Shared-memory layouts are still changing. SimpleNode manifest v3 and SharedHostDomain v3 (MINOSHD3) cannot open older segments, and writable secondary attach needs region layout v7, so upgrades mean recreating segments.
No isolation among processes attached to the same RW region; the trust boundary is UID/GID/namespace. LGPL-3.0 plus Bazel static linking means you must ship relinkable objects if you distribute.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Mino over TCPSHM, the other ZeroMQ-beater here and a small point-to-point connection library with sub-microsecond SHM round trips, when you need topic-based multi-process pipelines with IDL-typed messages, MPSC or broadcast fan-out, crash recovery and one API that bridges to TCP across hosts. Pick Zenoh instead when you need a mature, multi-language, routed pub/sub rather than a young C++/Linux-only single-host pipeline.
verified_claims_summary: The author ran a 2-round saturation test on an 8-vCPU Debian 13 KVM guest (CPU model undisclosed, bazel -c opt, C++20, compiler for this build not stated) with six processes and five hops, where every stage validates and copies the full payload. Mino SHM had mean p50 end-to-end latency of 1.8 ms vs 10.6 ms for Protobuf over ZeroMQ ipc:// PUSH/PULL at 256 B, 0.98 vs 1.97 ms at 64 KiB and 13.7 vs 26.9 ms at 1 MiB; a separate 50-message smoke run gave Mino loopback TCP 0.855 ms p50 vs 10.33 ms for ZeroMQ (which used ipc://, because all six roles shared one boot), and all percentiles include queueing delay.
status_note: Actively developed by one author (152 commits since 2026-07-26, last on 2026-09-13), with no releases and 2 stars. It is LGPL-3.0 and builds only with Bazel, so treat it as a candidate to evaluate rather than a dependency to vendor.
